## Approach

For this assignment, I used the Open Library Subjects API to ask which science fiction works have the most published editions and how that corresponds to when they were first published. I checked the API documentation and confirmed it's public and doesn't require an API key, so there are no credentials to protect. But I still identify myself with a User-Agent header as Open Library requests. I'll request the subject endpoint using the httr2 package, parse the JSON response, and flatten the nested work records into a tidy tibble using hoist()

## Challenges

I expect some hiccups. Each work has its authors stored as a nested list that I need to flatten into one column. Some records don't have authors or a first year of publication, so I leave those as NA instead of dropping them. The data is also crowdsourced, so the number of editions can vary. Finally, because I only asked for 100 works, my results are a sample and not the entire catalog.


## API selected

**Endpoint:** Open Library Subjects API

`GET https://openlibrary.org/subjects/science_fiction.json`

This endpoint returns works tagged with a subject, including title, authors, first publication year, and edition count. It is public and requires no account or API key, so there are no credentials to manage.

**Parameters used**

| Parameter | Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | 100 | Number of works to return |
| User-Agent header | course name and email | Open Library asks clients to identify themselves |

## Request and parsing

```{r}
library(httr2)
library(tidyverse)

resp <- request("https://openlibrary.org/subjects/science_fiction.json") |>
  req_url_query(limit = 100) |>
  req_user_agent("DataScienceHomework (sammymesa9@gmail.com)") |>
  req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
  req_perform()

dat <- resp_body_json(resp)
length(dat$works)
```

## Tidy data frame

```{r}
works <- tibble(w = dat$works) |>
  hoist(
    w,
    title      = "title",
    first_year = "first_publish_year",
    editions   = "edition_count",
    authors    = "authors",
    .simplify  = FALSE
  ) |>
     mutate(
    title      = map_chr(title, \(x) x %||% NA_character_),
    first_year = na_if(map_int(first_year, \(x) as.integer(x %||% NA)), 0L),
    editions   = map_int(editions, \(x) as.integer(x %||% NA)),
    author     = map_chr(
      authors,
      \(a) if (is.null(a) || length(a) == 0) NA_character_
           else paste(map_chr(a, \(p) p[["name"]] %||% NA_character_),
                      collapse = ", ")
    )
  ) |>
  select(title, author, first_year, editions) |>
  arrange(desc(editions))
```

```{r}
glimpse(works)
```

## Data-cleaning decisions

The JSON response stored each work’s authors as a nested list, so I used hoist() to pull out only the fields I needed (title, first publication year, edition count, and authors) and collapsed the author list into a single comma-separated string. Some works had no author or no first publication year, and I kept those records with NA values instead of dropping them, so no data was lost. I also found two works with a first publication year of 0, which is not a real date, so I converted those to NA as well. Finally, I coerced the year and edition counts to integers and discarded fields I didn’t need, such as cover IDs and availability details, to keep the data frame tidy.

## Analysis

### Most-published works

```{r}
works |> slice_head(n = 10)
```

```{r}
works |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = editions, y = fct_reorder(title, editions))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c3e50") +
  labs(
    title = "Science fiction works with the most editions",
    x = "Number of editions",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Does age relate to edition count?

```{r}
works |>
  filter(!is.na(first_year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(first_year, editions)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "First publication year vs. number of editions",
    x = "First published",
    y = "Editions (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Conclusion
The most published works are Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (3,548), Frankenstein (2,187), and The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (2,049). All of the top ten were also first published before 1950. From the scatter plot, works from the 1800s and early 1900s tend to have the most editions. In contrast, works published after 1950 tend to have about 100 or fewer. The oldest works in the sample, from the 1600s, have relatively few editions, so the relationship is not simply "older means more." Because this is just a sample of 100 works from a crowd sourced catalog, these results are a rough pattern, not a solid conclusion about all science fiction.
